questions.q: How is the present conditional built?
choices: The future stem plus the imperfect endings
The imperfect stem plus the future endings
The nous form of the present plus -ais
questions.why: Every stem you learned for the future works here unchanged: parler- gives je parlerais, and the irregulars ser-, aur-, ir-, fer-, viendr- are the same list.
Future stem parler- plus the imperfect ending -ais. The future je parlerai is one letter shorter, and the two are clearly different in speech.
The stem is aur-, as in the future, and the nous ending is -ions: aurions.
Falloir has the irregular stem faudr- and exists only in the third person singular: il faudrait, it would be necessary.

questions.q: « Demain, je partirai » versus « Si j'avais le temps, je partirais ». What separates them?
choices: Nothing — the two spellings are interchangeable
questions.why: One letter in writing, and an audible difference in speech. The conditional takes the imperfect endings, which is why it looks like -ais, -ait, -aient.

questions.q: Make it polite: « Je veux un café. » → « Je ___ un café. »
questions.why: Je veux un café is grammatically perfect and socially blunt. Je voudrais is the normal form in a shop, and this one substitution does more for how you come across than almost anything else.

questions.q: Soften the advice: « Tu dois te reposer. » → « Tu ___ te reposer. »
questions.why: Devoir in the conditional is exactly English should, and pouvoir in the conditional is exactly could: tu devrais, vous pourriez.

questions.q: What is the conditional doing in « Le président serait malade » ?
choices: Reporting unverified information — he is said to be ill
Stating a condition that was never met
questions.why: Journalism and gossip use the conditional where English says reportedly or apparently. Il y aurait vingt blessés works the same way.

questions.q: How is the past conditional built?
choices: Avoir or être in the conditional, plus the past participle
Avoir or être in the imperfect, plus the past participle
The conditional of the main verb, plus été
Aller in the conditional, plus an infinitive
questions.why: J'aurais mangé, je serais allé. Same auxiliary choice and same agreement rules as ever, with the auxiliary now in the conditional.

questions.q: « I should have told you » → « J'___ dû te le dire. »
questions.why: J'aurais dû is the single most useful past-conditional phrase: should have. Its twin is tu aurais pu, you could have.

questions.q: Past conditional: « elles (venir) ___ » (they would have come)
questions.why: Venir takes être, so the participle agrees with the feminine plural subject: venues.

questions.q: Build the sentence: I would have come if I had known.
questions.why: The conditional goes in the main clause and never after si, which takes the pluperfect. With the main clause first, no comma is needed.
Vouloir has the irregular stem voudr-, and the -ais ending marks it as conditional rather than future.

questions.q: Say this out loud: I should have told you.
questions.why: Regret and reproach are the past conditional's home ground, and the two pronouns stack in the order te le before the infinitive.

questions.q: Name five jobs the conditional does, with a short French example each.
a: 1. Politeness: Je voudrais un café. 2. Hypotheses: Ce serait génial. 3. The main clause of a si-sentence: Si j'avais de l'argent, j'achèterais une maison. 4. Unverified information: Le président serait malade. 5. Softened advice with devoir and pouvoir: Tu devrais te reposer, vous pourriez essayer. And in the past: j'aurais dû, tu aurais pu.
questions.why: One form, five jobs. What unites them is distance: the conditional holds the statement slightly away from being asserted as fact.
